This was spoken, great king, by the Blessed One, the god above gods, in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya: 'Monks, approach families like the moon—with body withdrawn, mind withdrawn, ever like a newcomer, and not presumptuous in families.'

Candaṅgapañho sattamo.

The seventh question on the qualities of the moon.

8. Sūriyaṅgapañho

8. The Question on the Qualities of the Sun

8. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘sūriyassa suriyassa (sī. syā. pī.) satta aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni satta aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, sūriyo sabbaṃ udakaṃ parisoseti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sabbakilesā anavasesaṃ parisosetabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

8. “Venerable Nāgasena, you say that 'seven qualities of the sun should be adopted.' What are those seven qualities that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, the sun completely dries up all water, so too, great king, a yogi, a practitioner, should completely dry up all defilements without remainder. This, great king, is the first quality of the sun to be adopted.

“Puna [M 0.0373] caparaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyo tamandhakāraṃ vidhamati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sabbaṃ rāgatamaṃ dosatamaṃ mohatamaṃ mānatamaṃ diṭṭhitamaṃ kilesatamaṃ sabbaṃ duccaritatamaṃ vidhamayitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, great king, just as the sun dispels darkness, so too, great king, a yogi, a practitioner, should dispel all the darkness of lust, the darkness of hatred, the darkness of delusion, the darkness of conceit, the darkness of views, the darkness of defilements, and all the darkness of misconduct. This, great king, is the second quality of the sun to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyo abhikkhaṇaṃ carati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena abhikkhaṇaṃ yoniso manasikāro kātabbo. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, great king, the sun moves constantly. Just so, great king, a yogi, a practitioner, should constantly apply wise attention. This, great king, is the third quality of the sun to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyo raṃsimālī, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena ārammaṇamālinā bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyassa catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, great king, the sun possesses a garland of rays. In the same way, great king, a yogi, a practitioner, should possess a garland of meditation objects. This, great king, is the fourth quality of the sun to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyo mahājanakāyaṃ santāpento carati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena ācārasīlaguṇavattappaṭipattiyā [P 0.0390] jhānavimokkhasamādhisamāpattiindriyabalabojjhaṅgasatipaṭṭhānasammappadhānaiddhipādehi sadevako loko santāpayitabbo. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyassa pañcamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, great king, the sun moves along, making the great multitude radiant. In the same way, great king, a yogi, a practitioner, should make the world with its deities radiant through virtuous conduct, moral qualities, and the practice of observances; through absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments; and through the faculties, powers, enlightenment factors, foundations of mindfulness, right exertions, and bases of psychic power. This, great king, is the fifth quality of the sun to be adopted.

“Puna [V 0.0359] caparaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyo rāhubhayā bhīto carati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena duccaritaduggativisamakantāravipākavinipātakilesajālajaṭite diṭṭhisaṅghāṭapaṭimukke kupathapakkhande kummaggapaṭipanne kumaggapaṭipanne (syā. ka.) satte disvā mahatā saṃvegabhayena mānasaṃ saṃvejetabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyassa chaṭṭhaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, great king, the sun moves in fear of the danger from Rāhu. Just so, great king, a yogi, a practitioner, seeing beings entangled in the net of misconduct, bad destinations, the uneven wilderness, the consequences of ruin, downfall, and defilements, cloaked in the thicket of views, rushing headlong onto wrong paths, committed to false ways, should stir his mind with great fear and spiritual urgency. This, great king, is the sixth quality of the sun to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyo kalyāṇapāpake dasseti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena indriyabalabojjhaṅgasatipaṭṭhānasammappadhānaiddhipādalokiyalokuttaradhammā dassetabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sūriyassa sattamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena vaṅgīsena –

Furthermore, great king, the sun reveals what is good and bad. Just so, great king, a yogi, a practitioner, should reveal mundane and supramundane qualities such as the faculties, the powers, the enlightenment factors, the foundations of mindfulness, the right exertions, and the bases of psychic power. This, great king, is the seventh quality of the sun to be adopted. This was spoken, great king, by the Elder Vaṅgīsa:

“‘Yathāpi sūriyo udayanto, rūpaṃ dasseti pāṇinaṃ;

Suciñca asuciñcāpi, kalyāṇañcāpi pāpakaṃ.

“Just as the rising sun reveals forms to living beings—both pure and impure, both good and bad—

“‘Tathā [M 0.0374] bhikkhu dhammadharo, avijjāpihitaṃ janaṃ;

Pathaṃ dasseti vividhaṃ, ādiccovudayaṃ yathā’”ti.

so too a monk who is a bearer of the Dhamma shows the various paths to beings shrouded in ignorance, like the rising of the sun.”

Sūriyaṅgapañho aṭṭhamo.

The eighth question on the qualities of the sun.

9. Sakkaṅgapañho

9. The Question on the Qualities of Sakka

9. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘sakkassa tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, sakko ekantasukhasamappito, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena ekantapavivekasukhābhiratena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sakkassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

9. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, 'Three qualities of Sakka should be adopted.' What are those three qualities to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, Sakka is entirely endowed with happiness, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should delight in the happiness of utter seclusion. This, great king, is the first quality of Sakka to be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sakko deve disvā paggaṇhāti, hāsamabhijaneti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena kusalesu dhammesu alīnamatanditaṃ santaṃ mānasaṃ paggahetabbaṃ, hāsamabhijanetabbaṃ, uṭṭhahitabbaṃ ghaṭitabbaṃ vāyamitabbaṃ[P 0.0391]. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sakkassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, great king, Sakka, upon seeing the devas, uplifts them and generates mirth. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should uplift a mind that is unsluggish, tireless, and peaceful in regard to wholesome states; he should generate mirth, and should be roused, striving, and energetic. This, great king, is the second quality of Sakka to be adopted.

“Puna [V 0.0360] caparaṃ, mahārāja, sakkassa anabhirati nuppajjati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena suññāgāre anabhirati na uppādetabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sakkassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena subhūtinā –

Furthermore, great king, discontent does not arise for Sakka. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should not generate discontent in an empty dwelling. This, great king, is the third quality of Sakka to be adopted. And this was stated, great king, by the Elder Subhūti:

“‘Sāsane te mahāvīra, yato pabbajito ahaṃ;

Nābhijānāmi uppannaṃ, mānasaṃ kāmasaṃhita’”nti.

“‘O great hero, since I went forth in your dispensation, I do not recall a thought connected with sensual desire ever arising in me.’”

Sakkaṅgapañho navamo.

The ninth question on the qualities of Sakka.

10. Cakkavattiṅgapañho

10. The Question on the Qualities of a Wheel-Turning Monarch

10. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘cakkavattissa cattāri aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni cattāri aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja[M 0.0375], cakkavattī catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi janaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena catassannaṃ parisānaṃ mānasaṃ saṅgahetabbaṃ anuggahetabbaṃ sampahaṃsetabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavattissa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

10. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, 'Four qualities of a wheel-turning monarch should be adopted.' What are those four qualities to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a wheel-turning monarch wins over the populace with the four bases of beneficence, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should win over, support, and gladden the minds of the four assemblies. This, great king, is the first quality of a wheel-turning monarch to be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavattissa vijite corā na uṭṭhahanti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena kāmarāgabyāpādavihiṃsāvitakkā na uppādetabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavattissa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena –

Furthermore, great king, in the realm of a wheel-turning monarch, thieves do not arise. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should not generate thoughts of sensual desire, ill will, and cruelty. This, great king, is the second quality of a wheel-turning monarch to be adopted. And this was stated, great king, by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods:

“‘Vitakkūpasame ca yo rato, asubhaṃ bhāvayate bhāvayatī (syā.) dha. pa. 350 dhammapade sadā sato;

Esa kho byantikāhiti, esa checchati mārabandhana’nti.

“‘One who delights in the stilling of thoughts, ever mindful, develops the perception of unattractiveness; this one will surely make an end, this one will sever Māra’s bond.’”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavattī divase divase samuddapariyantaṃ mahāpathaviṃ anuyāyati kalyāṇapāpakāni vicinamāno, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena kāyakammaṃ vacīkammaṃ manokammaṃ divase divase paccavekkhitabbaṃ ‘kiṃ nu kho me imehi tīhi ṭhānehi [V 0.0361] anupavajjassa divaso vītivattatī’ti. Idaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavattissa [P 0.0392] tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena aṅguttaranikāyavare –

Furthermore, great king, just as a wheel-turning monarch travels day by day over the great earth bounded by the ocean, investigating good and evil, so too, great king, should a yogi engaged in meditation review day by day his bodily, verbal, and mental conduct, reflecting: ‘Has my day passed without my being blameworthy in these three areas?’ This, great king, is the third quality of a wheel-turning monarch to be adopted. And this was stated, great king, by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the excellent Aṅguttara Nikāya:

‘Kathambhūtassa me rattindivā vītivattantīti vītipatantīti (sī. pī.) pabbajitena abhiṇhaṃ paccavekkhitabba’nti.

‘One who has gone forth should frequently reflect: “In what state do my days and nights pass?”’

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavattissa abbhantarabāhirārakkhā susaṃvihitā hoti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena abbhantarānaṃ bāhirānaṃ kilesānaṃ ārakkhāya satidovāriko ṭhapetabbo. Idaṃ[M 0.0376], mahārāja, cakkavattissa catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena –

Furthermore, great king, just as a wheel-turning monarch has his internal and external guards well-arranged, so too, great king, should a yogi engaged in meditation establish the gatekeeper of mindfulness to guard against internal and external defilements. This, great king, is the fourth quality of a wheel-turning monarch to be adopted. And this was stated, great king, by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods:

‘Satidovāriko, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako akusalaṃ pajahati kusalaṃ bhāveti, sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti, suddhamattānaṃ pariharatī’”ti.

‘With mindfulness as his gatekeeper, bhikkhus, a noble disciple abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome, abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless, and maintains himself in purity.’

Cakkavattiṅgapañho dasamo.

The tenth Question on the Qualities of a Wheel-Turning Monarch.

Pathavīvaggo tatiyo.

The third Chapter on Earth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Pathavī āpo ca tejo ca, vāyo ca pabbatena ca;

Ākāso candasūriyo ca, sakko ca cakkavattināti.

Earth, water, and fire, air and the mountain; space, the moon and sun, Sakka, and the wheel-turner.

4. Upacikāvaggo

The Chapter on the Termite

1. Upacikaṅgapañho

The Question on the Quality of the Termite

1. “Bhante [V 0.0362][M 0.0377] nāgasena, ‘upacikāya ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, upacikā upari chadanaṃ katvā attānaṃ pidahitvā gocarāya carati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sīlasaṃvarachadanaṃ katvā mānasaṃ pidahitvā piṇḍāya caritabbaṃ, sīlasaṃvarachadanena kho, mahārāja, yogī yogāvacaro sabbabhayasamatikkanto hoti. Idaṃ, mahārāja, upacikāya ekaṃ aṅgaṃ [P 0.0393] gahetabbaṃ, bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena upasenena vaṅgantaputtena –

4. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘One quality of the termite should be adopted.’ What is that one quality to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a termite makes a covering above itself, and having concealed itself, wanders for food, so too, great king, should a yogi engaged in meditation, having made a covering of virtuous restraint and concealed his mind, wander for alms. For with the covering of virtuous restraint, great king, the yogi engaged in meditation transcends all fear. This, great king, is the one quality of the termite to be adopted. And this was stated, great king, by the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta:”

“‘Sīlasaṃvarachadanaṃ, yogī katvāna mānasaṃ;

Anupalitto lokena, bhayā ca parimuccatī’”ti.

1. ‘Having made a covering of virtuous restraint for the mind, a yogi, unstained by the world, is released from fear.’

Upacikaṅgapañho paṭhamo.

1. The first Question on the Quality of the Termite.

2. Biḷāraṅgapañho

The Question on the Qualities of the Cat

2. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘biḷārassa dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, biḷāro guhāgatopi susiragatopi hammiyantaragatopi undūraṃ yeva pariyesati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena gāmagatenāpi araññagatenāpi rukkhamūlagatenāpi suññāgāragatenāpi satataṃ samitaṃ appamattena kāyagatāsatibhojanaṃ yeva pariyesitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, biḷārassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘two qualities of a cat should be adopted.’ What are these two qualities that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a cat, whether it has gone into a cave, a hole, or an inner chamber, seeks only a mouse, so too, great king, should a yogi engaged in meditation, whether he has gone to a village, to a forest, to the foot of a tree, or to an empty dwelling, constantly, continuously, and heedfully seek only the food of mindfulness directed to the body. This, great king, is the first quality of a cat that should be adopted.”

“Puna [V 0.0363] caparaṃ, mahārāja, biḷāro āsanne yeva gocaraṃ pariyesati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena imesu yeva pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu udayabbayānupassinā viharitabbaṃ ‘iti rūpaṃ iti rūpassa samudayo iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo, iti vedanā iti vedanāya samudayo iti vedanāya atthaṅgamo, iti saññā iti saññāya samudayo [M 0.0378] iti saññāya atthaṅgamo, iti saṅkhārā iti saṅkhārānaṃ samudayo iti saṅkhārānaṃ atthaṅgamo, iti viññāṇaṃ iti viññāṇassa samudayo iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti. Idaṃ, mahārāja, biḷārassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena –

2. “Furthermore, great king, a cat seeks its prey close by. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should dwell observing the arising and passing away in these very five aggregates subject to clinging thus: ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the passing away of form; such is feeling, such is the origin of feeling, such is the passing away of feeling; such is perception, such is the origin of perception, such is the passing away of perception; such are formations, such is the origin of formations, such is the passing away of formations; such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the passing away of consciousness.’ This, great king, is the second quality of a cat that should be adopted. And this was spoken by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods:”

“‘Na ito dūre bhavitabbaṃ, bhavaggaṃ kiṃ karissati;

Paccuppannamhi vohāre, sake kāyamhi vindathā’”ti.

2. ‘One should not be far from this; what will the peak of existence accomplish? In the present matter, within one’s own body, you should find it.’

Biḷāraṅgapañho dutiyo.

The second Question on the Qualities of the Cat.

3. Undūraṅgapañho

The Question on the Quality of the Mouse

3. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘undūrassa undurassa (syā. ka.) ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, undūro itocito ca vicaranto āhārūpāsīsako yeva carati, evameva kho, mahārāja[P 0.0394], yoginā yogāvacarena itocito ca vicarantena yoniso manasikārūpāsīsakeneva bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, undūrassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena upasenena vaṅgantaputtena –

“Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘one quality of a mouse should be adopted.’ What is that one quality that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a mouse, wandering here and there, moves about intent only on food, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation, wandering here and there, should be one who is intent only on wise attention. This, great king, is the one quality of a mouse that should be adopted. And this was spoken, great king, by the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta:”

“‘Dhammāsīsaṃ dhammasīsaṃ (sī. pī.) karitvāna, viharanto vipassako;

Anolīno viharati, upasanto sadā sato’”ti.

3. ‘Having made the Dhamma his chief, the one with insight dwells; unwavering he abides, ever peaceful and mindful.’

Undūraṅgapañho tatiyo.

3. The third Question on the Quality of the Mouse.

4. Vicchikaṅgapañho

The Question on the Quality of the Scorpion

4. “Bhante [V 0.0364] nāgasena, ‘vicchikassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, vicchiko naṅgulāvudho naṅgulaṃ ussāpetvā carati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena ñāṇāvudhena bhavitabbaṃ, ñāṇaṃ ussāpetvā viharitabbaṃ[M 0.0379]. Idaṃ, mahārāja, vicchikassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena upasenena vaṅgantaputtena –

“Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘one quality of the scorpion should be adopted.’ What is that one quality that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, the scorpion is armed with its tail and moves about with its tail raised, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should be armed with the weapon of knowledge and should dwell with knowledge raised. This, great king, is the one quality of the scorpion that should be adopted. And this was spoken, great king, by the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta:”

“‘Ñāṇakhaggaṃ gahetvāna, viharanto vipassako;

Parimuccati sabbabhayā, duppasaho ca so bhave’”ti.

4. ‘Having taken up the sword of knowledge, the one with insight dwells; he is freed from all fear and becomes difficult to assail.’

Vicchikaṅgapañho catuttho.

4. The fourth Question on the Quality of the Scorpion.

5. Nakulaṅgapañho

The Question on the Quality of the Mongoose

5. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘nakulassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, nakulo uragamupagacchanto bhesajjena kāyaṃ paribhāvetvā uragamupagacchati gahetuṃ, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena kodhāghātabahulaṃ kalahaviggahavivādavirodhābhibhūtaṃ lokamupagacchantena mettābhesajjena mānasaṃ anulimpitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, nakulassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena sāriputtena dhammasenāpatinā –

“Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘one quality of the mongoose should be adopted.’ What is that one quality that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a mongoose, when approaching a snake, first treats its body with a medicinal herb and then approaches to seize it, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation, when approaching a world that is full of anger and resentment, overcome by quarrels, disputes, arguments, and conflicts, should anoint his mind with the medicine of loving-kindness. This, great king, is the one quality of the mongoose that should be adopted. And this was spoken, great king, by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:”

“‘Tasmā sakaṃ paresampi, kātabbā mettabhāvanā;

Mettacittena pharitabbaṃ, etaṃ buddhāna sāsana’”nti.

5. ‘Therefore for oneself and others the development of loving-kindness should be done; one should pervade with a mind of loving-kindness—this is the teaching of the Buddhas.’

Nakulaṅgapañho pañcamo.

5. The fifth Question on the Quality of the Mongoose.

6. Jarasiṅgālaṅgapañho

The Question on the Qualities of the Old Jackal

6. “Bhante [V 0.0365][P 0.0395] nāgasena, ‘jarasiṅgālassa dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, jarasiṅgālo bhojanaṃ paṭilabhitvā ajigucchamāno yāvadatthaṃ āharayati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena bhojanaṃ paṭilabhitvā ajigucchamānena sarīrayāpanamattameva paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, jarasiṅgālassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena mahākassapena –

“Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘two qualities of the old jackal should be adopted.’ What are those two qualities that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, an old jackal, having obtained food, eats it without disgust to his satisfaction, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation, having obtained food, should consume it without disgust merely for the maintenance of the body. This, great king, is the first quality of the old jackal that should be adopted. And this was spoken, great king, by the Elder Mahākassapa:”

“‘Senāsanamhā oruyha, gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisiṃ;

Bhuñjantaṃ purisaṃ kuṭṭhiṃ, sakkacca naṃ upaṭṭhahiṃ.

‘Having descended from my lodging, I entered the village for alms; I respectfully approached and attended upon a man with leprosy who was eating.

“‘So [M 0.0380] me pakkena hatthena, ālopaṃ upanāmayi;

Ālopaṃ pakkhipantassa, aṅgulipettha chijjatha.

‘With his festering hand, he offered me a morsel of food; as he was placing the morsel, a finger broke off right there into the bowl.

“‘Kuṭṭamūlañca nissāya, ālopaṃ taṃ abhuñjisaṃ;

Bhuñjamāne vā bhutte vā, jegucchaṃ me na vijjatī’ti.

‘Leaning against the base of a wall, I ate that morsel; and neither while eating it nor after having eaten was there any disgust in me.’

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, jarasiṅgālo bhojanaṃ paṭilabhitvā na vicināti lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vāti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena bhojanaṃ paṭilabhitvā na vicinitabbaṃ ‘lūkhaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā sampannaṃ vā asampannaṃ vā’ti, yathāladdhena santussitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, jarasiṅgālassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena upasenena vaṅgantaputtena –

“Furthermore, great king, an old jackal, having obtained food, does not discriminate whether it is coarse or fine. So too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice, having obtained food, should not discriminate, thinking, ‘Is it coarse or fine, well-prepared or poorly prepared?’ He should be content with whatever he has received. This, great king, is the second quality of the old jackal that should be adopted. And this was spoken, great king, by the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta:

“‘Lūkhenapi ca santusse, nāññaṃ patthe rasaṃ bahuṃ;

Rasesu anugiddhassa, jhāne na ramate ramatī (sī. pī.) mano;

Itarītarena santuṭṭho santuṭṭhe (sī. pī.), sāmaññaṃ paripūratī’”ti.

‘One should be content even with coarse food, and not long for many other flavors. The mind of one greedy for flavors does not delight in jhāna. Content with whatever he gets, he fulfills the life of a recluse.’

Jarasiṅgālaṅgapañho chaṭṭho.

The Sixth Question on the Qualities of the Old Jackal.

7. Migaṅgapañho

7. The Question on the Qualities of the Deer

7. “Bhante [V 0.0366] nāgasena, ‘migassa tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, migo divā araññe carati, rattiṃ abbhokāse, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena divā araññe viharitabbaṃ, rattiṃ abbhokāse. Idaṃ, mahārāja, migassa [P 0.0396] paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

7. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘Three qualities of a deer are to be adopted.’ What are those three qualities that are to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a deer wanders in the forest by day and in the open at night, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice should dwell in the forest by day and in the open at night. This, great king, is the first quality of a deer to be adopted.

“Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena lomahaṃsanapariyāye –

“This too, great king, was spoken by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the Discourse that Causes the Hair to Stand on End:

‘So kho ahaṃ, sāriputta, yā tā rattiyo sītā hemantikā antaraṭṭhakā himapātasamayā antaraṭṭhake himapātasamaye (sī. pī. ka.), tathārūpāsu rattīsu rattiṃ abbhokāse viharāmi, divā vanasaṇḍe. Gimhānaṃ pacchime māse divā abbhokāse viharāmi, rattiṃ vanasaṇḍe’ti.

‘So I, Sāriputta, on those cold winter nights of the inter-seasonal eight-day period, at the time of snowfall, dwelt in the open at night and in a forest grove by day. And in the last month of summer, I dwelt in the open by day and in a forest grove at night.’

“Puna [M 0.0381] caparaṃ, mahārāja, migo sattimhi vā sare vā opatante vañceti vajjeti (ka.) palāyati, na kāyamupaneti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena kilesesu opatantesu vañcayitabbaṃ vajjayitabbaṃ (ka.) palāyitabbaṃ, na cittamupanetabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, migassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, just as a deer, when a spear or an arrow is descending upon it, eludes it and flees, not bringing its body near; so too, great king, when defilements descend upon him, the yogi devoted to the practice should elude them and flee, not bringing his mind near. This, great king, is the second quality of a deer to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, migo manusse disvā yena vā tena vā palāyati ‘mā maṃ te addasaṃsū’ti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena bhaṇḍanakalahaviggahavivādasīle dussīle kusīte saṅgaṇikārāme disvā yena vā tena vā palāyitabbaṃ ‘mā maṃ te addasaṃsu, ahañca te mā addasa’nti. Idaṃ, mahārāja, migassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena sāriputtena dhammasenāpatinā –

“Furthermore, great king, when a deer sees humans, it flees this way and that, thinking, ‘May they not see me.’ In the same way, great king, when a yogi devoted to the practice sees those who are quarrelsome, contentious, given to strife and dispute, immoral, lazy, and delighting in company, he should flee this way and that, thinking, ‘May they not see me, and may I not see them.’ This, great king, is the third quality of a deer to be adopted. This too, great king, was spoken by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:

“‘Mā me kadāci pāpiccho, kusīto hīnavīriyo;

Appassuto anācāro, sammato sameto (sī. pī.) ahu katthacī’”ti.

‘May I never, anywhere, be regarded as one with evil wishes, lazy, lacking energy, unlearned, or of bad conduct.’

Migaṅgapañho sattamo.

The Seventh Question on the Qualities of a Deer.

8. Gorūpaṅgapañho

8. The Question on the Qualities of an Ox

8. “Bhante [V 0.0367] nāgasena, ‘gorūpassa cattāri aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni cattāri aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, gorūpo sakaṃ gehaṃ na vijahati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sako kāyo na vijahitabbo ‘aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanavikiraṇaviddhaṃsanadhammo ayaṃ kāyo’ti. Idaṃ, mahārāja, gorūpassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

8. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘Four qualities of an ox are to be adopted.’ What are those four qualities that are to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, an ox does not abandon its own home, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice should not abandon his own body, reflecting: ‘This body is impermanent, subject to being anointed, massaged, broken up, scattered, and destroyed.’ This, great king, is the first quality of an ox to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, gorūpo ādinnadhuro sukhadukkhena dhuraṃ vahati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena ādinnabrahmacariyena [P 0.0397] sukhadukkhena yāva jīvitapariyādānā āpāṇakoṭikaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, gorūpassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, just as an ox, having taken up the yoke, bears the yoke through pleasure and pain, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice, having undertaken the holy life, should live the holy life through pleasure and pain until the end of life, to the very last breath. This, great king, is the second quality of an ox to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, gorūpo chandena ghāyamāno pānīyaṃ pivati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ anusiṭṭhi [M 0.0382] chandena pemena pasādena ghāyamānena paṭiggahetabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, gorūpassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, just as an ox, smelling with desire, drinks water, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice should receive the instruction of teachers and preceptors with desire, affection, and serene confidence. This, great king, is the third quality of an ox to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, gorūpo yena kenaci vāhiyamāno vahati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena theranavamajjhimabhikkhūnampi gihiupāsakassāpi ovādānusāsanī sirasā sampaṭicchitabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, gorūpassa catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena sāriputtena dhammasenāpatinā –

“Furthermore, great king, just as an ox, being driven by anyone, pulls its load, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice should accept advice and instruction from senior, junior, and middle monks, and even from lay devotees, with bowed head. This, great king, is the fourth quality of an ox to be adopted. This too, great king, was spoken by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:

“‘Tadahu pabbajito santo, jātiyā sattavassiko;

Sopi maṃ anusāseyya, sampaṭicchāmi matthake muddhanā (sī.).

‘Even if one gone forth on this very day, seven years old by birth, should advise me, I would accept it on my head.

“‘Tibbaṃ chandañca pemañca, tasmiṃ disvā upaṭṭhape;

Ṭhapeyyācariyaṭṭhāne, sakkacca naṃ punappuna’”nti.

‘Seeing in him intense desire and affection, I would attend upon him; I would place him in the position of a teacher, respectfully, again and again.’

Gorūpaṅgapañho aṭṭhamo.

The Eighth Question on the Qualities of an Ox.

9. Varāhaṅgapañho

9. The Question on the Qualities of a Boar

9. “Bhante [V 0.0368] nāgasena, ‘varāhassa dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, varāho santattakaṭhite santattakaṭhine (sī. pī.) gimhasamaye sampatte udakaṃ upagacchati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena dosena citte āluḷitakhalitavibbhantasantatte sītalāmatapaṇītamettābhāvanaṃ upagantabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, varāhassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

9. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘Two qualities of a boar are to be adopted.’ What are those two qualities that are to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a boar, when the scorching hot season has arrived, approaches the water, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice, when his mind is disturbed, agitated, confused, and burning with hatred, should resort to the cool, ambrosial, and sublime cultivation of loving-kindness. This, great king, is the first quality of a boar to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, varāho cikkhallamudakamupagantvā nāsikāya pathaviṃ khaṇitvā doṇiṃ katvā doṇikāya sayati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena [P 0.0398] mānase kāyaṃ nikkhipitvā ārammaṇantaragatena sayitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, varāhassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena piṇḍolabhāradvājena –

“Furthermore, great king, just as a boar, having approached muddy water, digs the earth with its snout, makes a hollow, and lies down in that hollow, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice, having placed the body in the mind, should lie down having entered into the meditation object. This, great king, is the second quality of a boar to be adopted. This too, great king, was spoken by the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja:

“‘Kāye kāyena (ka.) sabhāvaṃ disvāna, vicinitvā vipassako;

Ekākiyo adutiyo, seti ārammaṇantare’”ti.

‘Having seen the true nature in the body, the insight-practitioner investigates; alone, without a companion, he dwells within the meditation object.’

Varāhaṅgapañho navamo.

The Ninth Question on the Qualities of a Boar.

10. Hatthiṅgapañho

10. The Question on the Qualities of an Elephant

10. “Bhante [M 0.0383] nāgasena, ‘hatthissa pañca aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni pañca aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, hatthī nāma caranto yeva pathaviṃ dāleti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena kāyaṃ sammasamāneneva sabbe kilesā dāletabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, hatthissa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

10. “Venerable Nāgasena, you say, ‘Five qualities of an elephant should be adopted.’ What are those five qualities that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, an elephant while walking rends the earth, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to the practice, while contemplating the body, should rend all the defilements. This, great king, is the first quality of an elephant that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, hatthī sabbakāyeneva apaloketi, ujukaṃ yeva pekkhati, na disāvidisā viloketi, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sabbakāyena apalokinā [V 0.0369] bhavitabbaṃ, na disāvidisā viloketabbā, na uddhaṃ ulloketabbaṃ, na adho oloketabbaṃ, yugamattapekkhinā bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, hatthissa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, an elephant looks by turning its whole body; it looks straight ahead and does not glance in the various directions. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should look by turning his whole body; he should not glance in the various directions, he should not look up, he should not look down, but should be one who looks a yoke’s length ahead. This, great king, is the second quality of an elephant that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, hatthī anibaddhasayano gocarāyamanugantvā na tameva desaṃ vāsatthamupagacchati, na dhuvappatiṭṭhālayo, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena anibaddhasayanena bhavitabbaṃ, nirālayena piṇḍāya gantabbaṃ, yadi passati vipassako manuññaṃ patirūpaṃ ruciradese bhavaṃ maṇḍapaṃ vā rukkhamūlaṃ vā guhaṃ vā pabbhāraṃ vā, tattheva vāsamupagantabbaṃ, dhuvappatiṭṭhālayo na kātabbo. Idaṃ, mahārāja, hatthissa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, an elephant does not have a fixed resting place. Having gone to its feeding ground, it does not return to that same place to dwell; it does not have a permanent, established abode. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should not have a fixed resting place. He should go for alms without attachment. If the insight meditator sees a pleasant, suitable, and delightful place—a pavilion, the foot of a tree, a cave, or a mountain cleft—he should take up his dwelling right there, but he should not make it a permanent, established abode. This, great king, is the third quality of an elephant that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, hatthī udakaṃ ogāhitvā sucivimalasītalasalilaparipuṇṇaṃ kumuduppalapadumapuṇḍarīkasañchannaṃ mahatimahantaṃ [P 0.0399] padumasaraṃ ogāhitvā kīḷati gajavarakīḷaṃ, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sucivimalavippasannamanāviladhammavaravāripuṇṇaṃ vimuttikusumasañchannaṃ mahāsatipaṭṭhānapokkharaṇiṃ ogāhitvā ñāṇena saṅkhārā odhunitabbā vidhunitabbā, yogāvacarakīḷā kīḷitabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, hatthissa catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, an elephant, having entered the water, enters a great lotus pond filled with clear, pure, cool water and covered with blue and red lotuses and white water lilies, and plays the noble elephant’s sport. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should enter the great lotus pond of the establishments of mindfulness—filled with the excellent water of the Dhamma that is pure, clear, serene, and untroubled, and covered with the flowers of liberation—and with knowledge he should shake off and scatter the formations, playing the yogi’s sport. This, great king, is the fourth quality of an elephant that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, hatthī sato pādaṃ uddharati, sato pādaṃ nikkhipati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena satena sampajānena pādaṃ uddharitabbaṃ, satena sampajānena pādaṃ nikkhipitabbaṃ, abhikkamapaṭikkame samiñjanapasāraṇe sabbattha satena sampajānena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, hatthissa [M 0.0384] pañcamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena saṃyuttanikāyavare –

“Furthermore, great king, an elephant mindfully lifts its foot and mindfully places its foot. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should lift his foot with mindfulness and clear comprehension and place his foot with mindfulness and clear comprehension. In going forward and returning, in bending and stretching, in all things he should act with mindfulness and clear comprehension. This, great king, is the fifth quality of an elephant that should be adopted. And this, great king, was spoken by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya:”

“‘Kāyena saṃvaro sādhu, sādhu vācāya saṃvaro;

Manasā saṃvaro sādhu, sādhu sabbattha saṃvaro;

Sabbattha saṃvuto lajjī, rakkhitoti pavuccatī’”ti.

“‘Good is restraint in body, good is restraint in speech; good is restraint in mind, good is restraint in all things. The conscientious one, restrained in all things, is said to be protected.’”

Hatthiṅgapañho dasamo.Upacikāvaggo catuttho.

The tenth question on the qualities of the elephant is concluded. The fourth chapter, on the termite, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ [V 0.0370] –

The summary:

Upacikā biḷāro ca, undūro vicchikena ca;

Nakulo siṅgālo migo,

Gorūpo varāho hatthinā dasāti.

The termite and the cat, the mouse and the scorpion; the mongoose, jackal, deer, ox, boar, and elephant—these are the ten.

5. Sīhavaggo

The Chapter on the Lion

1. Sīhaṅgapañho

The Question on the Qualities of the Lion

1. “Bhante [V 0.0371][P 0.0400][M 0.0385] nāgasena, ‘sīhassa satta aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni satta aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, sīho nāma setavimalaparisuddhapaṇḍaro, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena setavimalaparisuddhapaṇḍaracittena byapagatakukkuccena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sīhassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

5. “Venerable Nāgasena, you say, ‘seven qualities of a lion should be adopted.’ What are those seven qualities that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a lion is white, stainless, utterly pure, and bright, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should have a mind that is white, stainless, utterly pure, and bright, with worry departed. This, great king, is the first quality of a lion that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sīho catucaraṇo vikkantacārī, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena caturiddhipādacaraṇena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sīhassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

1. “Furthermore, great king, the lion is four-footed and walks with a heroic gait. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should have the four bases of spiritual power as his feet. This, great king, is the second quality of a lion that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sīho abhirūparucirakesarī, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena abhirūparucirasīlakesarinā bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sīhassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

1. “Furthermore, great king, a lion has a handsome and beautiful mane. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should have the handsome and beautiful mane of virtuous conduct. This, great king, is the third quality of a lion that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sīho jīvitapariyādānepi na kassaci onamati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārapariyādānepi na kassaci onamitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sīhassa catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, even at the cost of its life, a lion does not bow down to anyone. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should not bow down to anyone even at the cost of his robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites for the sick. This, great king, is the fourth quality of a lion that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sīho sapadānabhakkho yasmiṃ okāse nipatati, tattheva yāvadatthaṃ bhakkhayati, na varamaṃsaṃ vicināti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sapadānabhakkhena bhavitabbaṃ, na kulāni vicinitabbāni, na pubbagehaṃ hitvā kulāni upasaṅkamitabbāni, na bhojanaṃ vicinitabbaṃ, yasmiṃ okāse kabaḷaṃ ādīyati, tasmiṃ yeva okāse [V 0.0372] bhuñjitabbaṃ sarīrayāpanatthaṃ sarīrayāpanamattaṃ (sī. pī.), na varabhojanaṃ vicinitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sīhassa pañcamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, a lion eats its prey systematically; where it falls, there it eats as much as it needs and does not seek out the choicest meat. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should go on his alms round systematically; he should not pick and choose families; he should not, having left a previous house, approach other families; he should not pick and choose his food. In whatever place he receives a morsel of food, he should eat it right there for the sustenance of his body; he should not seek out choice food. This, great king, is the fifth quality of a lion that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sīho asannidhibhakkho, sakiṃ gocaraṃ bhakkhayitvā na puna taṃ upagacchati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena asannidhikāraparibhoginā [M 0.0386] bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sīhassa chaṭṭhaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, a lion does not eat what is stored; having eaten its prey once, it does not approach it again. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should be one who partakes of things without storing them. This, great king, is the sixth quality of a lion that should be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ[P 0.0401], mahārāja, sīho bhojanaṃ aladdhā na paritassati, laddhāpi bhojanaṃ agadhito agathito (sī.) amucchito anajjhosanno paribhuñjati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena bhojanaṃ aladdhā na paritassitabbaṃ, laddhāpi bhojanaṃ agadhitena amucchitena anajjhosannena ādīnavadassāvinā nissaraṇapaññena paribhuñjitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sīhassa sattamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena saṃyuttanikāyavare theraṃ mahākassapaṃ parikittayamānena –

“Furthermore, great king, when a lion does not get food, it is not anxious; and when it gets food, it eats without greed, without infatuation, and without attachment. So too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should not be anxious when he does not get food; and when he gets food, he should eat it without greed, without infatuation, and without attachment, seeing the danger in it and with the wisdom of escape. This, great king, is the seventh quality of a lion that should be adopted. And this, great king, was spoken by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya, when extolling the Elder Mahākassapa:”

‘Santuṭṭhoyaṃ, bhikkhave, kassapo itarītarena piṇḍapātena, itarītarapiṇḍapātasantuṭṭhiyā ca vaṇṇavādī, na ca piṇḍapātahetu anesanaṃ appatirūpaṃ āpajjati, aladdhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ na paritassati, laddhā ca piṇḍapātaṃ agadhito amucchito anajjhosanno ādīnavadassāvī nissaraṇapañño paribhuñjatī’”ti.

“‘Bhikkhus, this Kassapa is content with any kind of almsfood, and he speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of almsfood. He does not, for the sake of almsfood, fall into what is unsuitable and improper. If he does not get almsfood, he is not anxious; and if he does get it, he partakes of it without being tied to it, infatuated with it, or attached to it, seeing the danger in it and possessing the wisdom of escape.’”

Sīhaṅgapañho paṭhamo.

The first question on the qualities of the lion is concluded.

2. Cakkavākaṅgapañho

The Question on the Qualities of the Ruddy Goose

2. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘cakkavākassa tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānīti”? “Yathā, mahārāja, cakkavāko yāva jīvitapariyādānā dutiyikaṃ na vijahati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena yāva jīvitapariyādānā yoniso manasikāro na vijahitabbo. Idaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavākassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘three qualities of the ruddy goose should be adopted.’ What are those three qualities that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, the ruddy goose does not abandon its mate until the end of its life, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in the practice should not abandon wise attention until the end of his life. This, great king, is the first quality of the ruddy goose that should be adopted.”

“Puna [V 0.0373] caparaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavāko sevālapaṇakabhakkho, tena ca santuṭṭhiṃ āpajjati, tāya ca santuṭṭhiyā balena ca vaṇṇena ca na parihāyati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena yathālābhasantoso karaṇīyo, yathālābhasantuṭṭho kho, mahārāja, yogī yogāvacaro na parihāyati sīlena, na parihāyati samādhinā, na [M 0.0387] parihāyati paññāya, na parihāyati vimuttiyā, na parihāyati vimuttiñāṇadassanena, na parihāyati sabbehi kusalehi dhammehi. Idaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavākassa [P 0.0402] dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

Furthermore, great king, the ruddy goose feeds on aquatic plants and moss, and finds contentment in that. Through this contentment, it does not decline in strength or complexion. In the same way, great king, a yogi devoted to spiritual practice should cultivate contentment with whatever he receives. Being content with what he receives, great king, the yogi devoted to spiritual practice does not decline in morality, does not decline in concentration, does not decline in wisdom, does not decline in liberation, does not decline in the knowledge and vision of liberation, and does not decline in any wholesome qualities. This, great king, is the second quality of the ruddy goose that should be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavāko pāṇe na viheṭhayati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena nihitadaṇḍena nihitasatthena lajjinā dayāpannena sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampinā bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, cakkavākassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsatampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena cakkavākajātake –

Furthermore, great king, the ruddy goose does not harm living beings. In the same way, great king, a yogi devoted to spiritual practice should have laid down the rod, laid down the weapon, be conscientious, compassionate, and sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings. This, great king, is the third quality of the ruddy goose to be adopted. This, great king, was also spoken by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the Cakkavāka Jātaka:

“‘Yo na hanti na ghāteti, na jināti na jāpaye;

Mettaṃso ahiṃsā (sī. pī.) sabbabhūtesu, veraṃ tassa na kenacī’”ti.

‘He who neither kills nor causes to kill, neither conquers nor causes to conquer, possessing loving-kindness towards all beings, has enmity with none.’

Cakkavākaṅgapañho dutiyo.

Here ends the Second Question on the Qualities of the Ruddy Goose.

3. Peṇāhikaṅgapañho

3. The Question on the Qualities of the Quail

3. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘peṇāhikāya dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, peṇāhikā sakapatimhi usūyāya chāpake na posayati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sakamane sakamano (ka.) kilese uppanne usūyāyitabbaṃ, satipaṭṭhānena sammāsaṃvarasusire pakkhipitvā manodvāre kāyagatāsati bhāvetabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, peṇāhikāya paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

3. “Venerable Nāgasena, you say that ‘two qualities of a female quail should be adopted.’ What are those two qualities that should be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a female quail, out of jealousy towards her own mate, does not nurture her young, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to spiritual practice should feel aversion towards the defilements that arise in his own mind. Having placed them into the aperture of right restraint by means of the foundations of mindfulness, mindfulness directed to the body should be developed at the mind-door. This, great king, is the first quality of a female quail that should be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, peṇāhikā pavane divasaṃ gocaraṃ caritvā sāyaṃ pakkhigaṇaṃ upeti attano guttiyā, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena ekakena pavivekaṃ sevitabbaṃ saṃyojanaparimuttiyā, tatra ratiṃ alabhamānena upavādabhayaparirakkhaṇāya saṅghaṃ osaritvā [V 0.0374] saṅgharakkhitena vasitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, peṇāhikāya dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, brahmunā sahampatinā bhagavato santike –

Furthermore, great king, just as a female quail, having wandered the forest for food during the day, approaches the flock of birds in the evening for her own protection, so too, great king, should a yogi devoted to spiritual practice resort to solitude for the sake of liberation from the fetters. But if he does not find delight in that, then for the sake of protection from the fear of blame, he should go to the Saṅgha and dwell under the Saṅgha's protection. This, great king, is the second quality of the female quail to be adopted. This was also spoken, great king, by Brahmā Sahampati in the presence of the Blessed One:

“‘Sevetha [M 0.0388] pantāni senāsanāni, careyya saṃyojanavippamokkhā;

Sace ratiṃ nādhigaccheyya tattha, saṅghe vase rakkhitatto satīmā’”ti.

‘One should resort to secluded lodging places, and practice for release from the fetters; if one finds no delight there, one should dwell in the Saṅgha, self-protected and mindful.’

Peṇāhikaṅgapañho tatiyo.

Here ends the Third Question on the Qualities of the Quail.

4. Gharakapotaṅgapañho

4. The Question on the Quality of the House Pigeon

4. “Bhante [P 0.0403] nāgasena, ‘gharakapotassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, gharakapoto paragehe vasamāno na tesaṃ kiñci bhaṇḍassa nimittaṃ gaṇhāti, majjhatto vasati saññābahulo, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena parakulaṃ upagatena tasmiṃ kule itthīnaṃ vā purisānaṃ vā mañce vā pīṭhe vā vatthe vā alaṅkāre vā upabhoge vā paribhoge vā bhojanavikatīsu vā na nimittaṃ gahetabbaṃ, majjhattena bhavitabbaṃ, samaṇasaññā paccupaṭṭhapetabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, gharakapotassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena cūḷanāradajātake –

4. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘one quality of the house pigeon should be adopted.’ What is that one quality to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a house pigeon living in another's home does not take note of any of their possessions, but dwells indifferent and abounding in perception, so too, great king, should a yogi devoted to spiritual practice, when visiting another's household, not take note of the women or men there, nor of their beds, chairs, clothes, ornaments, items of use, items of enjoyment, or various kinds of food. He should remain neutral and establish the perception of a recluse. This, great king, is the one quality of the house pigeon that should be adopted. This was also spoken, great king, by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the Cūḷanārada Jātaka:

“‘Pavisitvā parakulaṃ, pānatthaṃ bhojanāya vā pānesu bhojanesu vā (sī. pī.);

Mitaṃ khāde mitaṃ bhuñje, na ca rūpe manaṃ kare’”ti.

‘Having entered another's household for drink or for food, one should eat in moderation, consume in moderation, and not set one's mind on forms.’

Gharakapotaṅgapañho catuttho.

Here ends the Fourth Question on the Quality of the House Pigeon.

5. Ulūkaṅgapañho

5. The Question on the Qualities of the Owl

5. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘ulūkassa dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, ulūko kākehi paṭiviruddho, rattiṃ kākasaṅghaṃ gantvā bahūpi kāke hanati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena aññāṇena [V 0.0375] paṭiviruddho kātabbo, ekena raho nisīditvā aññāṇaṃ sampamadditabbaṃ, mūlato chinditabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, ulūkassa paṭhamaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

5. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘Two qualities of the owl are to be adopted.’ What are those two qualities to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, the owl is hostile to crows and, going into a flock of crows at night, kills many of them, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to spiritual practice should be opposed to ignorance. Sitting alone in seclusion, he should crush ignorance, cutting it off at the root. This, great king, is the first quality of the owl to be adopted.

“Puna [M 0.0389] caparaṃ, mahārāja, ulūko suppaṭisallīno hoti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena paṭisallānārāmena bhavitabbaṃ paṭisallānaratena. Idaṃ, mahārāja, ulūkassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena saṃyuttanikāyavare –

Furthermore, great king, the owl is fond of solitude. So too, great king, a yogi devoted to spiritual practice should delight in solitude and be fond of solitude. This, great king, is the second quality of the owl to be adopted. And this, great king, was spoken by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya:

“‘Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisallānārāmo paṭisallānarato “idaṃ dukkha”nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, “ayaṃ dukkhasamudayo”ti yathā bhūthaṃ pajānāti[P 0.0404], “ayaṃ dukkhanirodho”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, “ayaṃ dukkhanirodhagāminī paṭipadā”ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī’”ti.

‘Here, monks, a monk who delights in solitude, who is fond of solitude, understands as it really is: “This is suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the origin of suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the cessation of suffering”; he understands as it really is: “This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”’

Ulūkaṅgapañho pañcamo.

Here ends the Fifth Question on the Qualities of the Owl.

6. Satapattaṅgapañho

6. The Question on the Quality of the Woodpecker

6. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘satapattassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, satapatto ravitvā paresaṃ khemaṃ vā bhayaṃ vā ācikkhati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena paresaṃ dhammaṃ desayamānena vinipātaṃ bhayato dassayitabbaṃ, nibbānaṃ khemato dassayitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, satapattassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena piṇḍolabhāradvājena –

6. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘One quality of the woodpecker is to be adopted.’ What is that one quality to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, the woodpecker, by its call, indicates safety or danger to others, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to spiritual practice, while teaching the Dhamma to others, should show the lower realms as fearful and Nibbāna as safe. This, great king, is the one quality of the woodpecker to be adopted. And this, great king, was spoken by the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja:

“‘Niraye bhayasantāsaṃ, nibbāne vipulaṃ sukhaṃ;

Ubhayānetānatthāni dassetabbāni yoginā’”ti.

‘The fear and terror in hell, and the vast happiness in Nibbāna; a yogi should show both these matters.’

Satapattaṅgapañho chaṭṭho.

Here ends the Sixth Question on the Quality of the Woodpecker.

7. Vagguliṅgapañho

7. The Question on the Qualities of the Bat

7. “Bhante [V 0.0376] nāgasena, ‘vaggulissa dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni dve aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, vagguli gehaṃ pavisitvā vicaritvā nikkhamati, na tattha palibuddhati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā sapadānaṃ vicaritvā [M 0.0390] paṭiladdhalābhena khippameva nikkhamitabbaṃ, na tattha palibuddhena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, vaggulissa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

7. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘Two qualities of the bat are to be adopted.’ What are those two qualities to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a bat enters a house, moves about, and exits without becoming entangled there, so too, great king, a yogi devoted to spiritual practice, having entered a village for alms and gone from house to house in order, should quickly exit with whatever he has received, without becoming entangled there. This, great king, is the first quality of the bat to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, vagguli paragehe vasamāno na tesaṃ parihāniṃ karoti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena kulāni upasaṅkamitvā atiyācanāya vā viññattibahulatāya vā kāyadosabahulatāya vā atibhāṇitāya vā samānasukhadukkhatāya vā na tesaṃ koci vippaṭisāro karaṇīyo, napi tesaṃ mūlakammaṃ parihāpetabbaṃ, sabbathā vaḍḍhi yeva icchitabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, vaggulissa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā [P 0.0405] devātidevena dīghanikāyavare lakkhaṇasuttante –

“Furthermore, great king, a bat living in another’s house does not cause them any loss. So too, great king, when a yogi engaged in meditation approaches families, he should not cause them any regret through excessive begging, frequent requests, much bodily misconduct, excessive talk, or by sharing their joys and sorrows. Nor should their livelihood be diminished. In every way, only their growth should be wished for. This, great king, is the second quality of the bat to be adopted. And this, great king, was spoken by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the excellent Dīgha Nikāya, in the Lakkhaṇa Sutta:

“‘Saddhāya sīlena sutena buddhiyā, cāgena dhammena bahūhi sādhuhi;

Dhanena dhaññena ca khettavatthunā, puttehi dārehi catuppadehi ca.

“‘In faith, virtue, learning, and wisdom; in generosity and many good qualities of Dhamma; in wealth and grain, in fields and property, in sons and wives, and in four-footed animals;

“‘Ñātīhi mittehi ca bandhavehi, balena vaṇṇena sukhena cūbhayaṃ;

Kathaṃ na hāyeyyuṃ pareti icchati, atthasamiddhiñca panābhikaṅkhatī’”ti.

“‘In relatives, friends, and kinsmen; in strength, appearance, and both kinds of happiness—he wishes: ‘How might others not decline?’ and he longs for the accomplishment of their welfare.’”

Vagguliṅgapañho sattamo.

The Question on the Bat's Qualities is the seventh.

8. Jalūkaṅgapañho

8. The Question on the Leech's Quality

8. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘jalūkāya ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, jalūkā yattha allīyati, tattheva daḷhaṃ allīyitvā ruhiraṃ pivati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena yasmiṃ ārammaṇe [V 0.0377] cittaṃ allīyati, taṃ ārammaṇaṃ vaṇṇato ca saṇṭhānato ca disato ca okāsato ca paricchedato ca liṅgato ca nimittato ca daḷhaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā tenevārammaṇena vimuttirasamasecanakaṃ pātabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, jalūkāya ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena anuruddhena –

8. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said, ‘One quality of the leech is to be adopted.’ What is that one quality to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a leech, wherever it clings, clings firmly and drinks blood, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation, on whatever object his mind clings, should firmly establish that object in terms of its color, shape, direction, location, limits, distinguishing mark, and sign, and through that very object he should drink the pure, unadulterated taste of liberation. This, great king, is the one quality of the leech to be adopted. And this, great king, was spoken by the Elder Anuruddha:

“‘Parisuddhena [M 0.0391] cittena, ārammaṇe patiṭṭhāya;

Tena cittena pātabbaṃ, vimuttirasamasecana’”nti.

“‘With a purified mind, established on the object, with that mind one should drink the pure, unadulterated taste of liberation.’”

Jalūkaṅgapañho aṭṭhamo.

The Question on the Leech's Quality is the eighth.

9. Sappaṅgapañho

9. The Question on the Qualities of a Snake

9. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘sappassa tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, sappo urena gacchati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena paññāya caritabbaṃ, paññāya caramānassa kho, mahārāja, yogino cittaṃ ñāye carati, vilakkhaṇaṃ vivajjeti, salakkhaṇaṃ bhāveti. Idaṃ, mahārāja[P 0.0406], sappassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

9. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘three qualities of a snake should be adopted.’ Which are those three qualities to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a snake moves with its chest, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should conduct himself with wisdom. When conducting himself with wisdom, great king, the yogi’s mind moves in accordance with the right method, avoiding what is of a different nature and developing what is of the same nature. This, great king, is the first quality of a snake to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sappo caramāno osadhaṃ parivajjento carati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena duccaritaṃ parivajjentena caritabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sappassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, just as a snake, when moving about, avoids medicinal herbs, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should conduct himself by avoiding misconduct. This, great king, is the second quality of a snake to be adopted.

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, sappo manusse disvā tappati manussaṃ disvā kampati (ka.) socati cintayati, evameva kho mahārāja yoginā yogāvacarena kuvitakke, vitakketvā aratiṃ uppādayitvā tappitabbaṃ socitabbaṃ cintayitabbaṃ ‘pamādena me divaso vītināmito, na so puna sakkā laddhu’nti. Idaṃ, mahārāja, sappassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā bhallāṭiyajātake dvinnaṃ kinnarānaṃ –

“Furthermore, great king, just as a snake, upon seeing humans, feels distressed, grieves, and worries, so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation, having entertained unwholesome thoughts and having aroused discontent, should feel distressed, grieve, and worry: ‘Through negligence my day has passed, and it cannot be recovered.’ This, great king, is the third quality of a snake to be adopted. This was also spoken, great king, by the Blessed One in the Bhallāṭiya Jātaka, concerning two kinnaras:

“‘Mayekarattaṃ [V 0.0378] yamekarattiṃ (sī. pī.) vippavasimha ludda, akāmakā aññamaññaṃ sarantā;

Tamekarattaṃ tamekarattiṃ (sī. pī.) anutappamānā, socāma ‘sā ratti puna nahessatī’”ti.

“‘We spent one night apart, hunter, unwillingly remembering each other; regretting that single night, we grieve: ‘That night will not be again.’”

Sappaṅgapañho navamo.

The Question on the Snake's Qualities is the ninth.

10. Ajagaraṅgapañho

10. The Question on the Python's Quality

10. “Bhante [M 0.0392] nāgasena, ‘ajagarassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, ajagaro mahatimahākāyo bahūpi divase ūnūdaro dīnataro kucchipūraṃ āhāraṃ na labhati, aparipuṇṇo yeva yāvadeva sarīrayāpanamattakena yāpeti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yogino yogāvacarassa bhikkhācariyappasutassa parapiṇḍamupagatassa paradinnappāṭikaṅkhissa sayaṃgāhappaṭiviratassa dullabhaṃ udaraparipūraṃ āhāraṃ, api ca atthavasikena kulaputtena cattāro pañca ālope abhuñjitvā avasesaṃ udakena paripūretabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, ajagarassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena sāriputtena dhammasenāpatinā –

10. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘one quality of a python should be adopted.’ Which is that one quality to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a python, though having a massive body, may go many days with an empty belly, being quite distressed, not obtaining enough food to fill its stomach, and subsisting on just enough to sustain its body, so too, great king, for a yogi engaged in meditation, devoted to alms-seeking, dependent on the alms of others, expecting what is given by others, and abstaining from taking for himself, it is difficult to obtain enough food to fill his belly. Moreover, a clansman intent on the goal should, after eating four or five morsels, fill the rest with water. This, great king, is the one quality of a python to be adopted. This was also spoken, great king, by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:

“‘Allaṃ [P 0.0407] sukkhaṃ vā bhuñjanto, na bāḷhaṃ suhito siyā;

Ūnūdaro mitāhāro, sato bhikkhu paribbaje.

“‘Whether eating wet or dry food, one should not be excessively satisfied; with a less than full belly, moderate in eating, a mindful bhikkhu should go about.

“‘Cattāro pañca ālope, abhutvā udakaṃ pive;

Alaṃ phāsu vihārāya, pahitattassa bhikkhuno’”ti.

“‘Leaving four or five morsels uneaten, one should drink water; this is sufficient for a comfortable abiding for a bhikkhu with a resolute mind.’”

Ajagaraṅgapañho dasamo.

The Question on the Python's Quality is the tenth.

Sīhavaggo pañcamo.

The Fifth Chapter: The Lion.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Kesarī cakkavāko ca, peṇāhi gharakapotako;

Ulūko satapatto ca, vagguli ca jalūpikā;

Sappo ajagaro ceva, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

The lion and the ruddy goose, the peṇā and the house pigeon; the owl and the satapatta, the bat and the leech; the snake and the python—by these the chapter is declared.

6. Makkaṭakavaggo

The Chapter on the Spider

1. Panthamakkaṭakaṅgapañho

The Question on the Quality of the Roadside Spider

1. “Bhante [V 0.0379][M 0.0393] nāgasena, ‘panthamakkaṭakassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, panthamakkaṭako panthe makkaṭajālavitānaṃ katvā yadi tattha jālake laggati kimi vā makkhikā vā paṭaṅgo vā, taṃ gahetvā bhakkhayati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena chasu dvāresu satipaṭṭhānajālavitānaṃ katvā yadi tattha kilesamakkhikā bajjhanti, tattheva ghātetabbā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, panthamakkaṭakassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena anuruddhena –

6. “Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘one quality of the roadside spider should be adopted.’ Which is that one quality to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a roadside spider sets up a web-canopy on the road, and if any worm, fly, or moth gets caught in that web, it seizes and devours it—so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should set up the net-canopy of the establishments of mindfulness at the six sense doors. If any defilement-flies get caught there, they should be destroyed right there. This, great king, is the one quality of the roadside spider to be adopted. This was also spoken, great king, by the Elder Anuruddha:

“‘Cittaṃ niyame chasu dvāresu, satipaṭṭhānavaruttame;

Kilesā tattha laggā ce, hantabbā te vipassinā’”ti.

1. “‘One should restrain the mind at the six doors, in the supreme, best establishment of mindfulness; if defilements become caught there, they should be destroyed by one with insight.’”

Panthamakkaṭakaṅgapañho paṭhamo.

1. The Question on the Roadside Spider's Quality is the first.

2. Thanassitadārakaṅgapañho

The Question on the Quality of a Suckling Child

2. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘thanassitadārakassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti[P 0.0408]? “Yathā, mahārāja, thanassitadārako sadatthe laggati, khīratthiko rodati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sadatthe laggitabbaṃ, sabbattha dhammañāṇena bhavitabbaṃ, uddese paripucchāya sammappayoge paviveke garusaṃvāse kalyāṇamittasevane. Idaṃ, mahārāja, thanassitadārakassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena dīghanikāyavare parinibbānasuttante –

“Venerable Nāgasena, you said that ‘one quality of the suckling child should be adopted.’ Which is that one quality to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a suckling child is attached to his own welfare, crying when he wants milk—so too, great king, a yogi engaged in meditation should be attached to his own welfare. He should be endowed with knowledge of the Dhamma in all things: in learning, questioning, right application, seclusion, living with a teacher, and associating with good friends. This, great king, is the one quality of the suckling child to be adopted. This was also spoken, great king, by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the excellent Dīgha Nikāya, in the Parinibbāna Sutta:

“‘Iṅghaṃ [V 0.0380] tumhe, ānanda, sāratthe sadatthe (sī. pī.) ghaṭatha, sāratthe anuyuñjatha;

Sāratthe appamattā ātāpino pahitattā viharathā’”ti.

2. “‘Come now, Ānanda, strive for the essential goal, apply yourselves to the essential goal; dwell for the essential goal, heedful, ardent, and with resolute minds.’”

Thanassitadārakaṅgapañho dutiyo.

2. The Question on the Suckling Child's Quality is the second.

3. Cittakadharakummaṅgapañho

The Question on the Quality of the Tortoise with a Variegated Neck

3. “Bhante [M 0.0394] nāgasena, ‘cittakadharakummassa cittakathalakummassa (sī. pī.) ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba’nti yaṃ vadesi, katamaṃ taṃ ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabba”nti? “Yathā, mahārāja, cittakadharakummo udakabhayā udakaṃ parivajjetvā vicarati, tāya ca pana udakaṃ parivajjanāya āyunā na parihāyati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena pamāde bhayadassāvinā bhavitabbaṃ, appamāde guṇavisesadassāvinā. Tāya ca pana bhayadassāvitāya na parihāyati sāmaññā, nibbānassa santike upeti ṭhapeti (ka.). Idaṃ, mahārāja, cittakadharakummassa ekaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena dhammapade –

3. "Venerable Nāgasena, you say that 'one quality of the spotted tortoise should be adopted.' What is that one quality to be adopted?" "Just as, great king, a spotted tortoise, fearing water, avoids water while roaming about, and by that avoidance of water its lifespan is not diminished, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should be one who sees danger in negligence and sees the special advantage in diligence. And by seeing that danger, one does not fall away from the ascetic life but draws near to Nibbāna. This, great king, is the one quality of the spotted tortoise to be adopted. This was also spoken, great king, by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the Dhammapada:"

“‘Appamādarato bhikkhu, pamāde bhayadassi vā;

Abhabbo parihānāya, nibbānasseva santike’”ti.

"'A bhikkhu who delights in diligence, or who sees danger in negligence, is incapable of falling away; he is in the very presence of Nibbāna.'"

Cittakadharakummaṅgapañho catuttho.

The third question on the quality of the spotted tortoise.

4. Pavanaṅgapañho

4. The Question on the Qualities of the Forest

4. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘pavanassa pañca aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni pañca aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, pavanaṃ nāma asucijanaṃ paṭicchādeti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena paresaṃ aparaddhaṃ khalitaṃ paṭicchādetabbaṃ na vivaritabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, pavanassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

4. "Venerable Nāgasena, you say that 'five qualities of the forest should be adopted.' What are those five qualities to be adopted?" "Just as, great king, a forest conceals impure folk, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should conceal the offenses and lapses of others, not disclose them. This, great king, is the first quality of the forest to be adopted."

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, pavanaṃ suññaṃ pacurajanehi, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena [V 0.0381][P 0.0409] rāgadosamohamānadiṭṭhijālehi sabbehi ca kilesehi suññena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, pavanassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

"Furthermore, great king, just as a forest is empty of many people, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should be empty of all defilements—the tangle of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and views. This, great king, is the second quality of the forest to be adopted."

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, pavanaṃ vivittaṃ janasambādharahitaṃ, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehi anariyehi pavivittena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, pavanassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

"Furthermore, great king, just as a forest is secluded, free from the crowding of people, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should be secluded from evil, unwholesome, ignoble states. This, great king, is the third quality of the forest to be adopted."

“Puna [M 0.0395] caparaṃ, mahārāja, pavanaṃ santaṃ parisuddhaṃ, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena santena parisuddhena bhavitabbaṃ, nibbutena pahīnamānena pahīnamakkhena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, pavanassa catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

"Furthermore, great king, just as a forest is peaceful and pure, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should be peaceful and pure, quenched, with conceit abandoned, with contempt abandoned. This, great king, is the fourth quality of the forest to be adopted."

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, pavanaṃ ariyajanasaṃsevitaṃ, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena ariyajanasaṃsevitena bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, pavanassa pañcamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, bhagavatā devātidevena saṃyuttanikāyavare –

"Furthermore, great king, just as a forest is frequented by noble persons, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should be one who frequents noble persons. This, great king, is the fifth quality of the forest to be adopted. This was spoken, great king, by the Blessed One, the god beyond gods, in the excellent Saṃyutta Nikāya:"

“‘Pavivittehi ariyehi, pahitattehi jhāyibhi;

Niccaṃ āraddhavīriyehi, paṇḍitehi sahāvase’”ti.

"'One should associate with the wise who are secluded, noble, resolute, and meditative, with those who are ever energetic.'"

Pavanaṅgapañho catuttho.

The fourth question on the qualities of the forest.

5. Rukkhaṅgapañho

5. The Question on the Qualities of the Tree

5. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘rukkhassa tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni tīṇi aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, rukkho nāma pupphaphaladharo, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena vimuttipupphasāmaññaphaladhārinā bhavitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, rukkhassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

5. "Venerable Nāgasena, you say that 'three qualities of a tree should be adopted.' What are those three qualities to be adopted?" "Just as, great king, a tree bears flowers and fruit, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should bear the flower of liberation and the fruit of the ascetic life. This, great king, is the first quality of a tree to be adopted."

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, rukkho upagatānamanuppaviṭṭhānaṃ janānaṃ chāyaṃ deti, evameva kho[V 0.0382], mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena upagatānamanuppaviṭṭhānaṃ puggalānaṃ āmisappaṭisandhārena vā dhammappaṭisanthārena vā paṭisantharitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, rukkhassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

"Furthermore, great king, just as a tree gives shade to the people who have approached and come to it, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should extend a friendly welcome to the people who have approached and come to him, either a welcome with material things or a welcome with the Dhamma. This, great king, is the second quality of a tree to be adopted."

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, rukkho chāyāvemattaṃ [P 0.0410] na karoti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sabbasattesu vemattatā na kātabbā, coravadhakapaccatthikesupi attanipi samasamā mettābhāvanā kātabbā, ‘kinti ime sattā averā abyāpajjā abyāpajjhā (sī.) anīghā sukhī attānaṃ parihareyyu’nti. Idaṃ, mahārāja, rukkhassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena sāriputtena dhammasenāpatinā –

"Furthermore, great king, just as a tree makes no distinction in its shade, so too, great king, a yogi, one devoted to the practice, should make no distinction among any beings. He should develop loving-kindness equally towards all, towards a thief, a murderer, an enemy, and himself, thinking: ‘May these beings be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from trouble, and may they live happily!’ This, great king, is the third quality of a tree to be adopted. This was spoken, great king, by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:"

“‘Vadhake [M 0.0396] devadattamhi, core aṅgulimālake;

Dhanapāle rāhule ca, sabbattha samako munī’”ti.

"'Towards Devadatta the murderer, towards the thief Aṅgulimāla, towards the elephant Dhanapāla and towards Rāhula—the sage is impartial towards all.'"

Rukkhaṅgapañho pañcamo.

The fifth question on the qualities of the tree.

6. Meghaṅgapañho

6. The Question on the Qualities of a Cloud

6. “Bhante nāgasena, ‘meghassa pañca aṅgāni gahetabbānī’ti yaṃ vadesi, katamāni tāni pañca aṅgāni gahetabbānī”ti? “Yathā, mahārāja, megho uppannaṃ rajojallaṃ vūpasameti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena uppannaṃ kilesarajojallaṃ vūpasametabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, meghassa paṭhamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

6. “Venerable Nāgasena, you say, ‘Five qualities of a cloud are to be adopted.’ What are those five qualities to be adopted?” “Just as, great king, a cloud settles the arisen dust and dirt, so too, great king, a yogi, one engaged in meditation, should settle the arisen dust and dirt of the defilements. This, great king, is the first quality of a cloud to be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, megho pathaviyā uṇhaṃ nibbāpeti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena mettābhāvanāya sadevako loko nibbāpetabbo. Idaṃ, mahārāja, meghassa dutiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, just as a cloud extinguishes the heat of the earth, so too, great king, a yogi, one engaged in meditation, should cool the world with its devas through the development of loving-kindness. This, great king, is the second quality of a cloud to be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ, mahārāja, megho sabbabījāni viruhāpeti, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena sabbasattānaṃ saddhaṃ uppādetvā taṃ saddhābījaṃ tīsu sampattīsu ropetabbaṃ, dibbamānusikāsu sukhasampattīsu yāvaparamatthanibbānasukhasampatti. Idaṃ, mahārāja, meghassa tatiyaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, just as a cloud causes all seeds to sprout, so too, great king, a yogi, one engaged in meditation, having aroused faith in all beings, should plant that seed of faith in the three kinds of success: the blissful success of the divine and human realms, up to the blissful success of Nibbāna, the ultimate goal. This, great king, is the third quality of a cloud to be adopted.”

“Puna [V 0.0383] caparaṃ, mahārāja, megho ututo samuṭṭhahitvā dharaṇitalaruhe tiṇarukkhalatāgumbaosadhivanappatayo parirakkhati, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena yoniso manasikāraṃ nibbattetvā tena yoniso manasikārena samaṇadhammo parirakkhitabbo, yoniso manasikāramūlakā sabbe kusalā dhammā. Idaṃ, mahārāja, meghassa catutthaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ.

“Furthermore, great king, just as a cloud, arising in due season, protects the grasses, trees, vines, thickets, medicinal herbs, and forest trees growing on the surface of the earth, so too, great king, a yogi, one engaged in meditation, having generated wise attention, should protect the ascetic’s duties with that wise attention. For all wholesome states are rooted in wise attention. This, great king, is the fourth quality of a cloud to be adopted.”

“Puna caparaṃ[P 0.0411], mahārāja, megho vassamāno naditaḷākapokkharaṇiyo kandarapadarasarasobbhaudapānāni ca paripūreti udakadhārāhi, evameva kho, mahārāja, yoginā yogāvacarena āgamapariyattiyā dhammameghamabhivassayitvā adhigamakāmānaṃ mānasaṃ paripūrayitabbaṃ. Idaṃ, mahārāja, meghassa [M 0.0397] pañcamaṃ aṅgaṃ gahetabbaṃ. Bhāsitampetaṃ, mahārāja, therena sāriputtena dhammasenāpatinā –

“Furthermore, great king, just as a cloud, while raining, fills rivers, tanks, ponds, caves, chasms, lakes, pits, and wells with streams of water, so too, great king, a yogi, one engaged in meditation, having rained down the cloud of the Dhamma through his scriptural learning, should fill the minds of those who desire attainment. This, great king, is the fifth quality of a cloud to be adopted. This was said, great king, by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:”

“‘Bodhaneyyaṃ janaṃ disvā, satasahassepi yojane;

Khaṇena upagantvāna, bodheti taṃ mahāmunī’”ti.
